ww.Trichomonas vaginalis trophozoites: Trichomonas are motile, pear-shaped flagellates, a little larger than a white cell, usually among many neutrophils. Here the cells are plain epithelial cells with a stippled bacterial film and no protozoa, so this is not trichomoniasis.
ww.Candida pseudohyphae and budding yeast: Candida shows budding yeast and branching pseudohyphae, easiest to see after potassium hydroxide dissolves the cells. No hyphae are visible here; instead tiny bacteria blur the outline of each epithelial cell.
ww.Normal squamous cells with lactobacilli: Normal squamous cells keep a crisp, smooth edge, and the lactobacilli are long rods lying free beside them. A stippled coat of tiny coccobacilli that hides the cell border is what turns a normal cell into a clue cell.
ww.Cervicitis with many neutrophils: Cervicitis or another inflammatory vaginitis fills the field with neutrophils around clean-edged squamous cells. Bacterial vaginosis is not inflammatory: white cells are scarce, and the bacterial coat sits on the epithelial cells themselves.

look: Look at the two large, flat epithelial cells in the center. Their edges are fuzzy and stippled because a dense coat of tiny coccobacilli, mainly Gardnerella, clings to the membrane and hides the true border, while the nucleus still shows as a clear round spot. A normal squamous cell would have a sharp outline. This is the clue cell of bacterial vaginosis.

findings: Clue cell, lower left: a large squamous epithelial cell whose edge is blurred and stippled by a dense coat of small coccobacilli, mainly Gardnerella vaginalis and other anaerobes, so the true cell border cannot be traced.
Clue cell, upper right: a second epithelial cell overlaps the first and shows the same granular, stippled rim, which shows that the bacterial coating covers many cells in the smear rather than one.
Intact nucleus: each epithelial cell still shows a pale, round central nucleus, which marks it as an intact squamous cell; the bacteria cover the surface and do not invade the cell.

Sparse background: only a few small cells lie outside the clue cells, instead of the sheets of neutrophils seen in trichomoniasis or cervicitis, which fits the noninflammatory nature of bacterial vaginosis.
